title: Making edge on each trade
objectives: Compute the expected edge of a trade at your price.

screens.title: Pay £3 to roll
screens.prose: The interviewer offers a game. You pay £3 and roll a die, and they pay you the face in pounds. Betting games like this fill Zhou's green book and Crack's *Heard on the Street*.
screens.question: What do you expect to make per play, in pounds?

widget.accept: £0.50: the die averages £3.50 and you paid £3.
widget.label: Profit in pounds

hints.text: What does the die pay on average?
The average face is $(1 + 2 + \dots + 6)/6 = 3.5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the stake from the average payout.

byKey.sign: You took the payout from the stake. The game pays you £3.50 on average for £3.
byKey.stake: That is the average payout. You paid £3 to play.

explain.text: The die pays £3.50 on average and costs £3. So each play earns £0.50 on average. You should play as often as they let you.

screens.title: Play it many times
screens.prose: Play the £3 game many times. Each bar counts plays by your profit. The dashed line is your average profit so far.

state.caption: Run some plays and watch the mean line.

screens.question: After a thousand plays or more, where does your average profit per play sit?

options.why: Run 1,000 plays and read the mean line. It settles above 0, because the game favours you.
£3.50 is the average payout. Your profit is the payout minus the £3 stake.

options.text: It keeps swinging with no pattern
options.why: Single plays swing from −£2 to +£3. The average of many plays settles.

hints.text: Press Run 1,000 and read the dashed line.

feedback.correct: Near £0.50: the average settles on the edge.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run more plays and read the mean line.

explain.text: Each play is worth −£2 to +£3, each with chance 1/6. The average over many plays settles near £0.50. Single plays are noisy; the average is not.

screens.title: Edge
screens.prose: What a trade earns on average at its price is its **edge**. You sell at a price $p$ a contract worth $\mu$ on average. The interviewer buys 1 from you at 12 on three dice, fair value 10.5.
screens.question: What is your edge on this sale, per unit?

hints.text: A sale earns its price minus the value.
Edge 1.5 a unit.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the fair value from the sale price.

byKey.sign: You took the price from the value. For a sale, edge is price minus value.
byKey.price: That is the price. Edge is the price minus what the contract is worth.

explain.text: You sold for 12 a total worth 10.5 on average. Each unit earns 1.5 on average over every roll, though any one roll can win or lose more. For a purchase the edge is value minus price.

screens.title: Flip until a tail
screens.prose: Back to last lesson's coin game: flip until a tail, paid £1 for each head before it. Its fair value is £1. The interviewer now charges £1.20 to play.
screens.question: What is your edge per play, in pounds?

hints.text: Edge is the average payout minus the stake.
The average payout is £1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the £1.20 stake from the £1 average payout.

byKey.sign: You took the payout from the stake. You pay £1.20 for £1, so the edge is negative.
byKey.flips: You valued the game at £2, the average number of flips. It pays for heads only, £1 on average.
byKey.nopay: You counted the stake but not the payout. The game pays £1 on average.

explain.text: The game pays £1 on average and costs £1.20. So each play loses £0.20 on average. A negative edge is a reason to decline, or to sell the game instead.

screens.title: £2 on heads
screens.prose: Another game: stake £1.10 on a coin flip. Heads pays £2 and tails pays nothing.
screens.question: What is your edge per play, in pounds?

hints.text: Find the average payout first.
Half the time £2, half the time £0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The average payout is £1.

byKey.win: You used the payout on heads alone. Tails pays nothing half the time.
byKey.sign: You pay more than the game is worth, so the edge is negative.

explain.text: Heads pays £2 half the time, so the game is worth £1. You pay £1.10 for it. Each play loses £0.10 on average.

screens.title: A trader who knows nothing
screens.prose: You quote 9.5 at 11.5 on three dice, fair value 10.5. A trader who knows nothing trades with you four times, buying or selling at random.
screens.question: What is your P&L at fair after the four trades, in pounds?

widget.accept: £4: each trade earns £1, half the width.
widget.label: P&L in pounds

hints.text: What does each trade earn against 10.50?
Each purchase at 9.50 and each sale at 11.50 earns £1.
Four trades at £1: £4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each trade earns £1 against fair value.

byKey.width: You gave each trade the whole width, 2. A single trade earns half of it.
byKey.flat: Your position is not the point here. Each trade earned £1 on its own.
byKey.last: That is the running total before the last trade. Add the last £1.

explain.text: Each trade is £1 better than fair, half the width of 2. Against random flow, half the width is the edge of every trade. Four trades earn £4.

screens.title: It came up 14
screens.prose: A candidate sold 1 at 12 on three dice, fair value 10.5. The dice came up 14, so they lost £2. They say: "Selling at 12 was a bad trade."
screens.question: Was selling at 12 a good trade?

options.text: Yes: its edge was +1.5, and the 14 was bad luck.

options.why: You judged the trade by one outcome. The edge is the average over every roll, and that is +1.5.

options.text: Only if the next roll comes in under 12.
options.why: Each roll is new. The trade's value was fixed when it was made at 12.

options.text: Neither: wins and losses cancel out.
options.why: They do not cancel. Selling at 12 against 10.5 earns 1.5 on average.

hints.text: Is a trade judged by one roll or by the average over all rolls?
Most rolls land below 12, where the sale wins.
The edge was $12 - 10.5 = 1.5$; the loss was luck.

feedback.correct: A good trade with a bad outcome.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Judge the trade by its edge.

byKey.bad: You judged the trade by how this roll went. Repeat it a thousand times and it earns about £1,500.

explain.text: About 26% of rolls land above 12, so some sales at 12 lose. On average the sale earns 1.5, and that was known when it was made. Interviewers want the edge, not the outcome.

screens.title: Noise around the edge
screens.prose: Here are 100 plays of the £3 die game, drawn with seed 6. The path ends at £70, not the £50 the edge predicts. Each play's spread pushes the path around the edge line.
screens.question: What is the variance of one play's profit?

hints.text: Variance is $E[X^2] - E[X]^2$; the stake does not change it.
For one die, $E[X^2] = 91/6$ and $E[X]^2 = 49/4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the squared mean from the mean square.

byKey.mean: That is the mean payout. Variance measures the spread around it.
byKey.sd: That is the sd, the square root. The question asks for the variance.

explain.text: One play has variance $91/6 - 49/4 = 35/12$, about 2.92. Over 100 plays the sd is ten times 1.71, or £17.08, so £70 sits about one sd above £50. One play at 100 times the size has the same £50 edge, with an sd of £170.78.

screens.title: Edge, in general
screens.prose: You priced every trade against the fair value $\mu$. A sale at $p$ has edge $p - \mu$ and a purchase $\mu - p$. A game has edge $E[\text{payout}] - \text{stake}$. $$\text{edge}_{\text{sell}} = p - \mu, \qquad \text{edge}_{\text{buy}} = \mu - p.$$
screens.question: The interviewer offers to buy 1 from you at 10.5, your fair value on three dice. What is your edge?

widget.accept: 0: a trade at fair value earns nothing on average.
widget.label: Edge

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the fair value from the price.

byKey.width: You added your usual half-width. At 10.5 there is none.

explain.text: At fair value the edge is $10.5 - 10.5 = 0$. Such a trade is worth doing only to change your position. If you were long 3, selling at fair cuts your risk at no cost.

screens.title: Why the coin game is worth £1
screens.prose: Prove the coin game's fair value by looking at the first flip. Put the lines in order and leave out the one that stops too early.
screens.question: Order the derivation of $E$, the expected payout.

lines.text: Let $E$ be the expected payout of the game.
A first tail, chance $\tfrac12$: the game ends and pays £0.
A first head, chance $\tfrac12$: you bank £1 and the same game starts again, worth $E$.

lines.why: That stops after one flip. A head also restarts the game, which is worth $E$ again.

hints.text: Start by naming the unknown.
Split on the first flip, then write one equation.
Name $E$, the two cases, the equation, then solve.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split on the first flip before writing the equation.

byKey.d1: That stops after one flip. A head also restarts the game, which is worth $E$ again.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the one-flip shortcut belongs in the proof.

explain.text: After a head the coin has no memory, so the rest of the game is worth $E$ again. That gives $E = \tfrac12(1 + E)$, so $E = 1$. At £1.20 the edge is −£0.20, as you found.

screens.title: Edge in code
screens.prose: Write the two edges you have used. A game's edge must be exact, so build it from `Fraction` values.
screens.question: Complete `edge(side, price, fair)` and `game_edge(stake, payoff_fn, outcomes)`.

widget.starter:
from fractions import Fraction


def edge(side, price, fair):
    """Expected edge per unit of your trade.
    side is 'buy' or 'sell' (what you do)."""
    ...


def game_edge(stake, payoff_fn, outcomes):
    """Exact edge of paying stake to be paid
    payoff_fn(o), o drawn evenly from outcomes."""
    ...

tests.call: game_edge(Fraction(11, 10), lambda c: 2 if c == 'H' else 0, ['H', 'T'])

tests.setup: from itertools import product; rolls = list(product(range(1, 7), repeat=2))
from itertools import product; rolls = list(product(range(1, 7), repeat=2))

tests.call: game_edge(Fraction(1), lambda x: 10 if x == 6 else 0, range(1, 7))

widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests. `edge` must match exactly; `game_edge` must return a Fraction equal to the exact edge.

hints.text: A sale earns price minus fair; a purchase earns fair minus price.
Average `Fraction(payoff_fn(o))` over the outcomes.
Return the average payout minus `Fraction(stake)`.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check the sign for each side, and keep the game's edge a Fraction.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that each `...` is replaced.

explain.text: `edge` flips its sign with your side, so the same trade reads +1.5 sold and −1.5 bought. `game_edge` averages exact payouts, so the larger of two dice for £4 gives 17/36. A float would turn 1/36 into 0.02777...

screens.title: Edge, not one day's P&L
screens.prose: A market-making desk trades 2,000 times a day, 100 shares each time. Each trade has an edge of 0.5p a share. Yesterday the desk lost £300.
screens.question: What is the desk's expected P&L for a day, in pounds?

hints.text: Multiply trades, shares and edge.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply trades by shares by 0.5p, then turn pence into pounds.

byKey.shares: You left out the 100 shares in each trade.
byKey.pence: That is in pence. Divide by 100 for pounds.
byKey.yesterday: That is one day's outcome. The question asks for the expected P&L.

explain.text: The desk expects 100,000p, or £1,000, a day. Yesterday's −£300 is noise around that. Desks judge trades by their edge and judge P&L over many days.

ideas: Edge is what a trade earns on average at its price: selling at 12 against 10.5 earns 1.5.
A game's edge is its expected payout minus the stake; one outcome says little about it.
Against random flow each trade earns the half-width; many small edges beat one large bet.
summary.trap: Judging a trade by its outcome: a roll of 14 says nothing about the edge of a sale at 12.

quiz.prose: You pay £4 to roll two dice and are paid the larger face in pounds. The larger of two dice averages 161/36.
quiz.question: What is your edge per play, in pounds? Give four decimal places.

byKey.sign: You took the payout from the stake. The game is worth more than £4.
byKey.sum: You used the sum of two dice, 7. The game pays the larger face.

explain.text: The game is worth $161/36 \approx 4.4722$ and costs £4. The edge is $17/36$, about £0.47 a play. Play it.

quiz.prose: The interviewer sells you 2 at 9 on three dice, fair value 10.5.
quiz.question: What is your total edge on the trade?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A purchase earns fair minus price, times the size.

byKey.one: That is one unit. You bought 2.
byKey.sign: You bought below fair value, so the edge is positive.

explain.text: Each unit bought at 9 is worth 10.5, an edge of 1.5. Two units make 3. Size multiplies edge.

quiz.prose: You quote 13 at 15 on four dice, fair value 14. A trader who knows nothing buys or sells 1 at random.
quiz.question: What is your edge per trade?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each side sits half the width from 14.

byKey.width: You gave the whole width. Each trade is only on one side.

explain.text: A purchase at 13 earns 1 and a sale at 15 earns 1. Either way the trade earns the half-width. Random flow pays half the width a trade.

quiz.prose: You bought 1 at 9.5 on three dice, fair value 10.5. The dice came up 7.
quiz.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: The trade had edge +1; the 7 was bad luck.
The trade was bad: it lost 2.5.
options.why: You judged the trade by one roll. Its edge, fixed at 9.5, was +1.

options.text: The trade had no edge, because it lost.
options.why: Edge does not depend on the roll. Buying at 9.5 against 10.5 earns 1 on average.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Judge the trade at its price.

explain.text: Buying at 9.5 a total worth 10.5 has edge +1. This roll lost 2.5, and others win. The edge is what repeats.
